question: Select the sentence with the appropriate use of preposition.
option_1: They rise with the morning lark and labour till almost dark.
option_2: They rise with the morning lark and labour utmost almost dark.
option_3: They rise with the morning lark and labour by almost dark.
option_4: They rise with the morning lark and labour still almost dark.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. They rise with the morning lark and labour till almost dark.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The preposition "till" (same as "until") is used to show that an action continues up to a particular point of time. Here it means they keep working continuously right up to the time when it becomes almost dark.

• Rule: "Till/Until" + point of time is used for an action that goes on continuously up to that time, e.g., "He studied till midnight."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 is incorrect because "utmost" is an adjective/noun meaning "greatest possible" and is not a preposition of time; it cannot meaningfully combine with "almost dark".

• Option 3 is incorrect because "by" denotes a deadline — an action completed at or before a given time — not a continuous action lasting up to that time; "laboured by almost dark" is not idiomatic usage.

• Option 4 is incorrect because "still" is an adverb meaning "even now" and is not a preposition; it cannot grammatically precede "almost dark" in this structure.

NOTE

• Common time-prepositions tested by SSC: at (a point of time), on (a day/date), in (a period), till/until (continuation up to a time), by (deadline), since (starting point, used with Present Perfect), for (duration).

• Compare: "I will wait till 5 pm" (action continues up to 5) versus "I will finish the work by 5 pm" (action completed on or before 5).

question:
Select the most appropriate idiom that can substitute the italicised words in the given sentence.
He was sacked from his job because of a grave error on his part.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Himalayan blunder.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Himalayan blunder" means a very serious or huge mistake. (एक बहुत बड़ी गलती)
◦ Example: Ignoring the warning signs before the flood was a Himalayan blunder on the part of the administration.

• The phrase was famously used by Jawaharlal Nehru to describe India's misjudged China policy, and it has since become a standard English idiom for a colossal error, drawing on the sheer scale of the Himalayan mountains for emphasis.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Raining cats and dogs (मूसलधार बारिश होना): To rain very heavily.
◦ Example: We got drenched because it was raining cats and dogs.

• Option 2: Minding one's p's and q's (सावधानीपूर्वक व्यवहार करना): To be careful about one's manners and behaviour.

• Option 3: Picking holes in one's coat (दोष निकालना): To find fault with someone or criticise them unnecessarily.

NOTE

• Other idioms of "mistake/blame" often asked in SSC: "To err is human", "To pass the buck" (to shift blame to someone else), and "A slip of the tongue" (an unintentional verbal mistake).

question:
Select the most appropriate collocation to substitute the underlined word in the given sentence.
The banker warned me not to be careless from my ATM card.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. The banker warned me not to be careless with my ATM card.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The adjective "careless" collocates with the preposition "with" when referring to a lack of care in handling an object or possession — "careless with something".

• Rule — Collocation: Certain adjectives are fixed to specific prepositions by convention (usage), not by logic alone; "careless with" is one such standard pairing meaning negligent in handling something.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "careless beside" is incorrect because "beside" means "next to" (a position) and does not collocate with "careless".

• Option 3: "careless across" is incorrect because "across" indicates movement/position from one side to another and has no collocational link with "careless".

• Option 4: "careless on" is incorrect because "on" is not the conventional preposition used with "careless" in this sense.

NOTE

• Other common adjective + preposition collocations tested by SSC: careless about (unconcerned regarding), angry with (a person), angry at (a situation), married to, afraid of, proud of, capable of, good at.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word.
Beowulf was praised for his valour displayed in the battlefield.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Cowardice.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Valour" means great courage or bravery, especially in battle. (वीरता / साहस) Its opposite, "Cowardice", means a lack of courage; timidity in the face of danger. (कायरता)
◦ Example: Beowulf was praised for his valour, while the knight who fled the battlefield was mocked for his cowardice.

• Rule — Antonyms: To find the correct antonym, first fix the precise sense of the given word (here, "bravery in danger") and then eliminate options that are close in meaning or unrelated, keeping only the word with the exact opposite sense.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Forbearance (सहनशीलता): Patient self-control; restraint in provocation — related to patience, not to bravery, so it is not the opposite of valour.

• Option 2: Erudition (विद्वता): Extensive knowledge gained from study; this relates to learning, not to courage.

• Option 4: Idiosyncrasy (विचित्रता/निजी स्वभाव): A peculiar or eccentric habit or mannerism of an individual; unrelated to bravery.

NOTE

• Synonyms of "Valour": bravery, gallantry, fortitude, heroism, intrepidity.

• Other antonym pairs frequently asked by SSC: brave × timid, courageous × cowardly, bold × diffident, heroic × craven.

question:
Select the most appropriate idiom that can substitute the italicised words in the given sentence.
I have been a vegetarian for a very long time.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. donkey's years.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "donkey's years" means a very long time. (बहुत लंबे समय से)
◦ Example: I haven't visited my hometown in donkey's years.

• The phrase is believed to have originated as a pun on "donkey's ears", which are long, combined with the popular belief that donkeys live for a long time.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: Duck in a thunderstorm (घबराया हुआ व्यक्ति): To describe someone who looks bewildered, confused or agitated.

• Option 3: Die in harness (कर्तव्य निभाते हुए मरना): To die while still actively working, in service till the very end.

• Option 4: Damocles' sword (सिर पर मंडराता खतरा): An imminent, ever-present danger or threat looming over someone.

NOTE

• Other idioms meaning "a long time" often asked in SSC: "In a month of Sundays", "Once in a blue moon" (meaning rarely, not "a long time" — a commonly confused pair), and "Till the cows come home" (for a very long/indefinite time).

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
A very expensive and elaborately built tomb
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Mausoleum.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Mausoleum" means a very expensive and elaborately built tomb, usually a grand stone building housing the remains of one or more important people. (एक भव्य और महंगी समाधि)
◦ Example: The Taj Mahal is a magnificent mausoleum built by Shah Jahan for his wife Mumtaz Mahal.

• Rule — One-word substitution: These questions require matching a defining phrase to a single precise word; focus on the key distinguishing features in the phrase — here "very expensive" and "elaborately built" point specifically to a grand tomb, not any burial place.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: Cemetery — a general place/ground where the dead are buried; it does not imply an expensive or elaborate single structure.

• Option 3: Mosque — a Muslim place of worship, unrelated to a tomb.

• Option 4: Masterpiece — a work of outstanding artistry or skill; it need not be a tomb at all.

NOTE

• Related one-word substitutes often confused: Cenotaph (a monument to someone buried elsewhere, e.g. a war memorial), Sepulchre (a small room/tomb for burial), Necropolis (a large ancient cemetery).

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
Every nook and corner of the house were unclean.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. of the house was unclean.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The subject of the sentence is "Every nook and corner". When a subject is preceded by "every" (or "each"), it is treated as singular even if it is a compound phrase joined by "and", and therefore takes a singular verb.

• Rule — Subject-Verb Agreement with "every/each": "Every" and "each" make a compound subject grammatically singular; use singular verbs like "was", "is", "has", not plural ones like "were", "are", "have".
◦ Example: Every boy and girl was present at the function.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "of a house was unclean" is incorrect because it changes "the house" to "a house", altering the meaning by making it indefinite/general instead of referring to the specific house in question.

• Option 2: "by the house were unclean" is incorrect both for the wrong preposition ("by" instead of "of") and for retaining the plural verb "were".

• Option 3: "to the house were unclean" is incorrect for the same two reasons — wrong preposition "to", and incorrect plural verb "were".

NOTE

• Other subjects that always take a singular verb: each, every, either, neither, everyone, everybody, everything, someone, anyone, no one, nobody — e.g., "Neither of the answers is correct."

• Compound subjects joined by "and" are normally plural (e.g., "Ram and Shyam are friends"), EXCEPT when preceded by every/each, or when they together denote a single idea/person (e.g., "Bread and butter is my favourite breakfast").

question:
Select the correct direct form of the given sentence.
John said that he was there to resolve that fight for them.
option_1: John says, "I am here to resolve this fight for you."
option_2: John said to me, "You are here to resolve this fight for you."
option_3: John said, "I am here to resolve this fight for you."
option_4: John said, "I was here to resolve this fight for you."
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. John said, "I am here to resolve this fight for you."

IMPORTANT POINTS

• In the given indirect (reported) sentence, "John said that he was there to resolve that fight for them", the reporting verb "said" is in the simple past, and the reported verb "was" is also in the past — this past tense in the indirect speech was produced by back-shifting the original present tense used by the speaker.

• Rule — Indirect to Direct conversion: When converting back to direct speech, (i) the reporting verb outside the inverted commas keeps the same tense as given (here, "said" remains "said"); (ii) the tense inside the inverted commas is restored to what the speaker actually said — the past tense "was" is converted back to the present tense "am"; (iii) pronouns are reversed to the speaker's own point of view: "he" → "I", and "them" (the listeners) → "you"; (iv) the demonstrative "that" reverts to "this" and "there" reverts to "here" since the speaker is describing his own immediate situation.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because the reporting verb has wrongly been changed to the present tense "says", whereas the question specifies "said" (past tense) and it must remain unchanged.

• Option 2 is incorrect because it wrongly adds "to me" (not present in the original) and wrongly keeps the subject as "You" instead of "I" — it is John himself who is speaking about his own presence, not addressing "you" as the doer.

• Option 4 is incorrect because it retains the past tense "was" inside the quotation marks instead of restoring it to the present tense "am", which is what John would actually have said.

NOTE

• Pronoun changes while converting indirect to direct speech: he/she → I, they → we/they (context-based), them/him/her → you/me (based on who is speaking/addressed).

• Place and time word reversals: there → here, that → this, those → these, then → now, that day → today, the next day → tomorrow, the previous day → yesterday.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Tyranny
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Autocracy.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Tyranny" means cruel, oppressive and unjust use of power or authority by a ruler. (अत्याचार / निरंकुश शासन) "Autocracy" means a system of government by a single ruler with absolute, unrestricted power, which is the closest match among the given options because such unchecked rule is typically oppressive in the same way tyranny is.
◦ Example: The people finally revolted against the king's tyranny/autocracy.

• Rule — Synonym questions: Choose the option that is closest in core meaning to the given word among the choices offered, even if it is not a perfect one-to-one match, since SSC synonym sets often include the "nearest" rather than an exact synonym.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: Compassion (करुणा): Sympathy and concern for the suffering of others — the very opposite quality of a tyrant.

• Option 3: Social (सामाजिक): Relating to society or living in a community; unrelated to oppressive rule.

• Option 4: Discordance (मतभेद/असंगति): Disagreement or lack of harmony; unrelated to tyranny.

NOTE

• Other words related to "Tyranny": despotism, dictatorship, oppression, subjugation.

• Antonym of "Tyranny": democracy, liberty, justice.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
Rearing of silk worms is called horticulture.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. sericulture.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Sericulture" specifically means the rearing of silkworms for the production of raw silk. (रेशम के कीड़ों को पालना)
◦ Example: Many farmers in Karnataka earn their living through sericulture.

• Rule — Branches of "culture" (rearing/cultivation) words: SSC frequently tests this family of words, each referring to the rearing/cultivation of a specific thing; identifying the exact subject (here, "silk worms") is key to picking the correct term.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Pisciculture — the rearing/breeding of fish, not silkworms.

• Option 2: Agriculture — the general science/practice of cultivating crops and raising livestock; too broad and not specific to silkworms.

• Option 4: Apiculture — the keeping/rearing of bees for honey, not silkworms.

NOTE

• Other related "-culture" words: Horticulture (cultivation of gardens/fruits/flowers/vegetables), Viticulture (cultivation of grapes), Aquaculture (farming of aquatic organisms), Floriculture (cultivation of flowers).

question:
Select the correct active form of the given sentence.
The memorial event is expected to be attended by thousands of people.
option_1: Thousands of people was expected to attend the memorial event.
option_2: Thousands of people are expected to attending the memorial event.
option_3: Thousands of people had expected to attending the memorial event.
option_4: Thousands of people are expected to attend the memorial event.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Thousands of people are expected to attend the memorial event.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence "The memorial event is expected to be attended by thousands of people" is in the passive voice, Present Simple with a modal-like structure ("is expected to be + V3").

• Rule — Passive with "expected to be + V3": Active: Subject + is/are + expected + to + V1 + Object. Passive: Object + is/are + expected + to + be + V3 + by + Subject. To convert passive to active, reverse this: the passive subject "the memorial event" becomes the object, the agent "thousands of people" (introduced by "by") becomes the new subject, and "to be attended" changes to "to attend".

• Applying the rule: agent "thousands of people" (plural) becomes the subject, so the auxiliary is "are"; "to be attended" becomes "to attend"; and the original subject "the memorial event" becomes the object.
◦ Active: Thousands of people are expected to attend the memorial event.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "was expected" wrongly changes the tense to past, and "to attend" should not be preceded by a past-tense finite verb here since the passive original is in the present tense.

• Option 2 is incorrect because "expected to attending" uses the wrong non-finite form; after "to" the base form of the verb ("attend") must be used, not the gerund ("attending").

• Option 3 is incorrect for the same reason — "had expected to attending" is doubly wrong: it wrongly uses the past perfect "had expected" and the incorrect gerund form "attending" after "to".

NOTE

• With infinitive constructions ("expected to", "supposed to", "likely to", "going to"), the verb that follows "to" must always be in its base form (V1), never the "-ing" form.

• Passive structures with modal-type expressions are commonly tested: "is said to be", "is believed to be", "is known to be" — all follow the same active-passive transformation pattern.

question:
Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word in the following sentence.
Tyrany must be dead to attain harmony, tranquillity, and serenity.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. tyrany.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Tyranny" (with a double "n"), meaning cruel and oppressive rule; the word printed in the sentence as "Tyrany" is missing one "n" and is therefore misspelt.

• Spelling key: TYRAN + N + Y — remember the double "n" before the final "y", as in related words like "tyrant" and "tyrannical".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "tranquillity" is correctly spelt (note the double "l" — the British spelling convention doubles the "l" before a suffix).

• Option 3: "serenity" is correctly spelt — the state of being calm and peaceful.

• Option 4: "harmony" is correctly spelt — a state of agreement or pleasant combination.

NOTE

• Commonly confused double-letter spellings in SSC exams: tranquillity (British) vs. tranquility (American), committee, necessary (one "c", two "s"), occurrence, embarrass.

question: Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Kecthup.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Ketchup" — a thick sauce, typically made from tomatoes, used as a condiment; the word printed as "Kecthup" has the "t" and "c" transposed and is therefore misspelt.

• Spelling key: KET + CHUP — remember the sequence "t" before "c" ("ket-chup"), not "c" before "t".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Movement" is correctly spelt — the act or process of moving.

• Option 3: "Precise" is correctly spelt — exact and accurate.

• Option 4: "Flashy" is correctly spelt — showy or gaudy in a vulgar way.

NOTE

• Other frequently misspelt everyday words tested by SSC: restaurant, February, questionnaire, government, definitely, occasion, liaison.

question:
Select the most appropriate phrasal verb to fill in the blank.
The company's profits were low and they were forced to __________ staff.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. lay off.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrasal verb "lay off" means to dismiss employees, usually temporarily or due to lack of work/low profits. (कर्मचारियों को नौकरी से निकालना)
◦ Example: Due to the recession, the factory had to lay off hundreds of workers.

• Rule: The context "profits were low and they were forced to ___ staff" clearly signals reduction of workforce due to financial difficulty, which is the exact meaning of "lay off".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "lisp off" — not a standard/meaningful phrasal verb in this context; "lisp" relates to a speech defect, unrelated to employment.

• Option 3: "lay on" means to provide or supply something (e.g., a meal, entertainment); it does not mean to dismiss staff.

• Option 4: "lie on" means to rest in a horizontal position on something; it is unrelated to employment and also confuses "lie" (to rest) with "lay" (to place/put).

NOTE

• Commonly confused phrasal verbs with "lay": lay off (dismiss from job), lay out (arrange/plan), lay down (state a rule; or give up, as in "lay down arms"), lay up (store for future use; or be confined due to illness).

• Related phrasal verbs about jobs: take on (hire), let go (dismiss, softer term), fire/sack (dismiss, informal).

question:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them may contain an error. Select the part that contains the error from the given options. If you don't find any error, mark 'No error' as your answer.
After seeing that Shreya / was in trouble, / Rahul quietly stepped up to help.
option_1: Rahul quietly stepped up to help
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. No error.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "After seeing that Shreya was in trouble, Rahul quietly stepped up to help" is grammatically correct in every part: the subordinate clause "After seeing that Shreya was in trouble" is properly constructed, and the main clause "Rahul quietly stepped up to help" correctly follows with proper subject-verb agreement and tense.

• Rule — Error-spotting "No error" questions: Before selecting a part as an error, check subject-verb agreement, tense consistency, correct preposition/conjunction usage, and word order in each segment; if none of these have an actual mistake, "No error" must be selected rather than forcing a fault onto a correct segment.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Rahul quietly stepped up to help" is correct — proper subject, adverb placement, and past tense verb "stepped".

• Option 2: "After seeing that Shreya" is correct — "after seeing that" correctly introduces the subordinate clause explaining the reason/circumstance.

• Option 3: "was in trouble" is correct — singular subject "Shreya" correctly takes the singular past-tense verb "was".

NOTE

• In "No error" type questions, always check each segment individually against core rules (agreement, tense, preposition, article, parallel structure) before concluding there is no mistake — SSC deliberately includes some genuinely correct sentences to test whether candidates force an error where none exists.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select 'No substitution'.
Santa Claus stays at the North Pole when he isn't out deliver gifts for Christmas.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. out delivering.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence uses the auxiliary "isn't" (is + not), which requires the main verb to be in the present participle (-ing) form to form the present continuous tense — "is/isn't + V-ing".

• Rule — Present Continuous Tense: Subject + is/am/are (+ not) + V-ing. Here, "when he isn't out delivering gifts" correctly means "when he is not [currently engaged in] delivering gifts".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "out to delivering" is incorrect because "to" followed by the gerund "delivering" is an ungrammatical mixture — "to" should be followed by the base verb ("to deliver"), not the "-ing" form.

• Option 3: "No substitution" is incorrect because the original phrase "out deliver" is grammatically incomplete/incorrect as it stands (a bare base verb cannot follow "isn't" to express continuous action), so a substitution is indeed required.

• Option 4: "out of deliver" is incorrect because "deliver" here is being used as a bare verb, but "out of" must be followed by a noun/gerund, and even then, "out of deliver" is not meaningful.

NOTE

• After forms of "be" (is/am/are/was/were), the following main verb must take the -ing form to express a continuous/progressive action.

• Common confusion: "out delivering" (continuous action, correct here) versus "out to deliver" (expressing purpose/intention, a different structure — e.g., "He is out to deliver a strong performance").

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Guilty
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Innocent.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Guilty" means having committed a wrong or crime; responsible for an offence. (दोषी) Its direct opposite is "Innocent", meaning free from guilt; not responsible for a wrong or crime. (निर्दोष)
◦ Example: The jury found the accused guilty, but his lawyer maintained that he was innocent.

• Rule — Antonyms: Look for the word that expresses the exact opposite state or quality of the given word; here, the opposite of "having committed wrong" is "having committed no wrong", which is precisely "innocent".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Remnant (शेष भाग): A small remaining part of something; unrelated to guilt or innocence.

• Option 3: Nonchalant (उदासीन/बेपरवाह): Calm and casual, showing a lack of concern or anxiety; unrelated in meaning.

• Option 4: Omnipotent (सर्वशक्तिमान): Having unlimited power; unrelated to guilt.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "Guilty": culpable, blameworthy, at fault. Other synonyms of "Innocent": blameless, guiltless, faultless.

• Commonly confused antonym pair: "guilty" (having done wrong) vs. "guilt-ridden" (feeling guilty) — SSC tests the plain adjective form.

question:
Select the option that is similar in meaning to the underlined word.
The president's concern for the homeless people was superficial and ended as soon as the media left the event.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Shallow.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Superficial" means existing or occurring at or on the surface only; not thorough, deep, or genuine. (सतही/दिखावटी) "Shallow" carries the same core sense of lacking depth or genuineness, making it the closest match. (उथला/छिछला)
◦ Example: His superficial/shallow concern for the poor vanished the moment the cameras stopped rolling.

• Rule — "Similar in meaning" questions: Read the underlined word in its sentence context first (here, describing an insincere, short-lived "concern" that ended once the media left), and then pick the option that best matches that specific contextual sense.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: Derogatory (अपमानजनक): Expressing a low opinion of someone; disrespectful — this describes insulting language, not a lack of depth.

• Option 3: Regardless (परवाह किए बिना): Without regard or consideration for something; not a match for "not genuine/not deep".

• Option 4: Insubstantial (अपर्याप्त/निराधार): Lacking solidity or substance; while related, it is less precise than "shallow" for describing a person's insincere concern in this context.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "Superficial": cursory, perfunctory, skin-deep. Antonyms: profound, genuine, deep-rooted.

• Commonly tested word family: superficial (adj.) → superficiality (noun) → superficially (adverb).

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
A place where coins and medals are made.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Mint.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Mint" means a place, typically authorized by the government, where coins and medals are officially manufactured. (टकसाल)
◦ Example: The Royal Mint has produced British coins for centuries.

• Rule — One-word substitution: Focus on the precise activity described — "where coins and medals are made" specifically denotes manufacture of currency/metal tokens, a meaning unique to "mint".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Office — a place of business or administrative work; far too general and unrelated to coin-making.

• Option 3: Mine — a place from which minerals or metals (such as ore) are extracted from the earth, not where finished coins are manufactured.

• Option 4: Barn — a farm building for storing grain or housing livestock; unrelated.

NOTE

• Commonly confused pair: "Mint" (where coins/medals are made) vs. "Mine" (where raw minerals are extracted) — SSC often places these as distractors together, as seen in this very question.

• Other related one-word substitutes: Treasury (a place where public/government money is kept), Vault (a secure room for storing valuables).

question:
Select the correct passive voice form for the given sentence.
My brother likes football.
option_1: Football was liked by my brother.
option_2: Football is like by my brother.
option_3: Football was like by my brother.
option_4: Football is liked by my brother.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Football is liked by my brother.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "My brother likes football" is an assertive sentence in the Simple Present Tense.

• Rule — Simple Present Tense:
◦ Active: Subject + V1/V5 (base/-s form) + Object
◦ Passive: Object + is/am/are + V3 + by + Subject

• Applying the rule: the object "football" becomes the subject; being singular/uncountable, it takes the auxiliary "is"; the verb "likes" becomes the past participle "liked"; and "my brother" becomes the agent introduced by "by".
◦ Passive: Football is liked by my brother.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Football was liked by my brother" is incorrect because "was" wrongly shifts the sentence into the Simple Past Tense, changing the intended present-tense meaning.

• Option 2: "Football is like by my brother" is incorrect because the past participle "liked" has been wrongly written as the base form "like"; the passive structure always requires V3.

• Option 3: "Football was like by my brother" is incorrect for two reasons combined — the wrong past tense auxiliary "was" and the incorrect base form "like" instead of the past participle "liked".

NOTE

• The passive voice of the Simple Present Tense always uses "is/am/are + V3"; never the base verb form after the auxiliary.

• Verbs like "like", "love", "hate", "know", "believe" (stative verbs) are commonly tested for passive conversion because learners often forget to change them to their past participle form.

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

The monastery in Tawang has recently undergone (1)__________ and bright paintings (2)__________ it walls. Dances and ceremonial celebrations are held in the (3)__________, the most important of which is held on the night of Buddha Purnima, the full moon on which the Buddha was born, (4)__________ enlightenment and died. To reach Tawang, you drive for 12 hours from Assam's Tezpur town, a major Indian Forces base. The best seasons the visitor can choose for coming to Tawang is (5)__________ September to November.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. renovation.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank describes something the monastery has "recently undergone", followed shortly after by a mention of "bright paintings" on its walls — this points to restoration/repair work being done on the building, which is precisely what "renovation" means: the process of repairing and restoring a building to good condition.

• Rule — Cloze passage strategy: Read beyond the blank to the rest of the sentence (here, "and bright paintings [adorn] it walls") for contextual clues; a monastery undergoing renovation would naturally also be freshly painted, so the two ideas logically connect.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "innovation" means introducing something new; it does not fit the idea of a building being physically restored/repaired.

• Option 2: "depreciation" means a decrease in value over time; this contradicts the positive image of a monastery being freshly painted and cared for.

• Option 3: "termination" means an ending or conclusion of something; it does not logically fit "the monastery has recently undergone termination".

NOTE

• Words related to "renovation": restoration, refurbishment, revamping, remodelling — all commonly tested in cloze passages about heritage sites and old buildings.

To reach Tawang, you drive for 12 hours from Assam's Tezpur town, a major Indian Forces base. The best seasons the visitor can choose for coming to Tawang is (5)__________ September to November.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. adorn.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The verb "adorn" means to decorate or add beauty to something, which correctly fits the sense that bright paintings decorate/beautify the monastery's walls.

• Rule — Cloze passage strategy: Match the blank to a verb that logically connects its subject ("bright paintings") with its object ("it walls") — paintings can decorate/adorn walls, giving a coherent, positive image consistent with the rest of the sentence about renovation.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "expose" means to uncover or reveal something hidden, typically something negative; it does not fit paintings' relationship with walls.

• Option 2: "rectify" means to correct or put right a fault; walls are not "corrected" by paintings.

• Option 3: "adore" means to love or admire deeply; it is used for people/things one feels affection for, not for describing paintings' placement on walls.

NOTE

• Commonly confused pair: "adorn" (to decorate) vs. "adore" (to love/admire) — both look and sound similar but have very different meanings, and SSC frequently sets them as distractors together, as in this very question.

To reach Tawang, you drive for 12 hours from Assam's Tezpur town, a major Indian Forces base. The best seasons the visitor can choose for coming to Tawang is (5)__________ September to November.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. courtyard.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A "courtyard" is an open area enclosed by walls or buildings, commonly found within monasteries and temples, where communal activities such as dances and ceremonial celebrations are traditionally held.

• Rule — Cloze passage strategy: Since the passage is about a Buddhist monastery, the space for its "dances and ceremonial celebrations" must be a place naturally associated with a monastery — a courtyard fits both the setting (a religious complex) and the described activity.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "churchyard" specifically refers to the grounds surrounding a Christian church, often used as a burial ground; it does not belong to a Buddhist monastery setting.

• Option 3: "shipyard" is a place where ships are built or repaired; completely unrelated to a monastery.

• Option 4: "junkyard" is a place where scrap and discarded items are collected; entirely unrelated to a place for celebrations.

NOTE

• Compound words with "-yard" tested by SSC: backyard, farmyard, graveyard, vineyard, courtyard — each denotes an enclosed/open area for a specific purpose, and their prefixes give away their precise meaning.

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

The monastery in Tawang has recently undergone (1)__________ and bright paintings (2)__________ it walls. Dances and ceremonial celebrations are held in the (3)__________, the most important of which is held on the night of Buddha Purnima, the full moon on which the Buddha was born, (4)__________ enlightenment and died. To reach Tawang, you drive for 12 hours from Assam's Tezpur town, a major Indian Forces base. The best seasons the visitor can choose for coming to Tawang is (5)__________ September to November.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. attained.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The verb "attained" means achieved or reached (a state or goal) through effort, which correctly describes how the Buddha reached enlightenment through spiritual effort — a well-known fact referred to as "attaining enlightenment".

• Rule — Cloze passage strategy / collocation: "Enlightenment" collocates naturally with the verb "attain" in both religious and general English usage ("to attain enlightenment/nirvana/salvation"), making it the standard, expected word here.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "displayed" means to show or exhibit something; enlightenment is an inner spiritual state that is reached, not "displayed".

• Option 3: "transferred" means to move something from one place/person to another; enlightenment cannot be "transferred" in this sense — it is personally attained.

• Option 4: "received" means to be given or to accept something from an external source; it does not carry the sense of achievement through one's own spiritual effort that "attained" conveys.

NOTE

• Common fixed collocations tested in cloze passages: attain enlightenment/success/salvation, achieve a goal/target, accomplish a task/mission, reach a conclusion/decision.

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

The monastery in Tawang has recently undergone (1)__________ and bright paintings (2)__________ it walls. Dances and ceremonial celebrations are held in the (3)__________, the most important of which is held on the night of Buddha Purnima, the full moon on which the Buddha was born, (4)__________ enlightenment and died. To reach Tawang, you drive for 12 hours from Assam's Tezpur town, a major Indian Forces base. The best seasons the visitor can choose for coming to Tawang is (5)__________ September to November.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. between.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The preposition "between" is used when referring to a range or relationship involving two specific points/items — here, the two named months, September and November, mark the two ends of the ideal visiting period.

• Rule — Between vs. Among: "Between" is used for two entities/points (e.g., between September and November); "among" is used for more than two entities (e.g., among the five friends). Since exactly two months are named, "between" is the grammatically correct choice.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "about" means "approximately" or "concerning"; it does not correctly express a range bounded by two specific months.

• Option 2: "beside" means "next to" (a position); it cannot logically combine with a range of months.

• Option 4: "among" is used for more than two items/entities, but here only two specific months (September and November) are being referred to, so "among" is grammatically incorrect.

NOTE

• Classic SSC distinction: "between the two of them" vs. "among the three of them" — always count the number of items/persons referred to before choosing between "between" and "among".

• "Between" is also idiomatically fixed in phrases like "between you and me", "read between the lines".
